meaning: The Kohathite age and the unity among brothers – a connection between Levitical service and divine blessing over the community
description: The number 133 appears in the Bible as the lifespan of Kohath, son of Levi and ancestor of the Levitical Kohathite clan (Exod 6:18). Kohath was the father of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, and through Amram he became an ancestor of both Moses and Aaron. The Kohathites were given the most sacred duty among the Levites: to carry the ark of the covenant and the most holy items in the tabernacle (Num 4:4–15). That Kohath’s long life is noted in the text highlights his importance as a link between the patriarch Levi and the Mosaic revelation. Symbolically, the number 133 is also connected to Psalm 133, one of the Songs of Ascents (Shir HaMa'alot), where David praises the value of fellowship and unity with the words "See how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity". Together these texts point to a recurring biblical theme: the blessing upon those who serve God in unity and solidarity.

versions.meaning: The number 133 is linked to Psalm 133, which celebrates the unity and harmony among brothers who dwell together.
versions.description: In biblical tradition, Psalm 133 is one of the most well-known "Songs of Ascents" (Shir HaMa'alot), where David praises the value of community and unity with the words "Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity". In Jewish tradition, this psalm is interpreted as an expression of the ideal community in Israel and the divine blessing that follows from solidarity. The number 133 thus has a symbolic connection to unity, brotherhood, and God's blessing over a harmonious community.
versions.reason: [major] The description lacks the reference to Exodus 6:18, where the number 133 appears explicitly as Kohath's lifespan. This is the only direct occurrence of the number 133 in the Bible and should be included.; [minor] Psalm 133 is relevant as a symbolic association, but the description gives the impression that the number 133 primarily concerns Psalm 133. Kohath's lifespan and his role as the ancestor of the Levites (and thus of Moses and Aaron) should be included as a central part of the description.; [minor] It would be beneficial to add a footnote about Kohath's significance in Levitical tradition and about Psalm 133's liturgical use as a pilgrimage psalm, to provide depth without breaking the flow.

footnotes.text: The Kohathite clan (the Kohathites) were responsible for the most holy objects in the tabernacle, including the ark of the covenant, the table of showbread, the lampstand, and the altars. They were not allowed to touch the holy objects directly but had to carry them on poles after Aaron and his sons had covered them (Num 4:4–20).

Psalm 133 is part of the collection Shir HaMa'alot (Psalms 120–134), pilgrimage psalms that were sung by those who went up to Jerusalem during the major festivals. In Jewish liturgy, Psalm 133 is traditionally read before the afternoon prayer on the Sabbath.

In rabbinic tradition, the anointing oil that flows down over Aaron's beard (Ps 133:2) is interpreted as a picture of how God's blessing flows from the holy place out to the entire community. Some rabbis connect this to the Kohathite clan, who served at the most holy place.
